question: A junior risk analyst at a Frankfurt bank’s EUR 2.4 billion hedge fund allocation programme is preparing a training slide for newly hired analysts. The slide sorts sample due diligence questions into the four themes used to evaluate a hedge fund manager: strategy, ownership, track record and investment management. Which of the following pairings of question and theme is most accurate?

options.A: “Are most of the staff who generated the past results still employed by the firm?”: strategy.
options.B: “Has the fund ever been soft or hard closed, or returned capital to investors?”: strategy.
options.C: “Do the traders, portfolio managers and research analysts hold equity in the firm?”: investment management.
options.D: “Did former employers find the manager to be a leader or a follower?”: track record.

solution:
Junior analyst sorting sample due diligence questions into the four manager evaluation themes.

**Concept and theory**

Schweser organises manager evaluation into four themes. Strategy asks what the manager does and how: style, current themes, how the portfolio has evolved, turnover and liquidity, loss-limiting mechanisms, quantitative models, short sales, derivatives, trade execution, private investments, the trade-off between current returns and fund growth, and whether the fund has ever been closed or returned capital. Ownership asks whether the investment team (traders, portfolio managers, research analysts) hold equity in the firm. question:
The CIO of a Japanese corporate pension plan with JPY 310 billion in alternatives is drafting the strategy section of an interview guide for an equity long/short manager. A consultant proposes four entries:

I. Ask what triggers a reversal or an exit decision, and whether those triggers are hard coded into the risk management process or are just guidelines.

II. Ask whether stop losses are used at the position level, the portfolio level or both, and whether they are always executed or are subject to exceptions.

III. Ask whether short sales are used as hedges or as alpha generators, and screen out any manager who answers that they are used as both.

IV. Ask how proprietary models are developed and back-tested, but leave out how they are allocated capital or decommissioned, since those are business model questions.

Which of the entries are consistent with the strategy questions an investor can consider when evaluating the manager?

options.A: I only
options.B: I and III only
options.C: II and IV only
options.D: I and II only

solution:
CIO drafting strategy interview entries on exit triggers, stop losses, short sales and models.

GARP’s strategy list is designed to make the manager explain how the portfolio is actually run, not just what the pitch book says. Several questions probe the mechanics of discipline. question:
A treasury analyst at a Singapore insurer is reviewing a global macro fund in which the insurer already holds SGD 150 million. Her notes on the manager are summarised below.

| Item | Observation |
|---|---|
| Assets under management | SGD 0.9 billion three years ago; SGD 4.2 billion today |
| Investor relations headcount | Increased from 2 to 9 |
| Fund status | Has never been closed to new subscriptions |
| Management and incentive fees | 1.5% and 20%, unchanged since launch |

Her concern is that continued subscriptions may dilute the returns earned by existing investors such as the insurer. Which strategy question most directly addresses her concern?

options.A: How does the firm manage the conflict between generating returns for existing investors and growing assets under management, and is the strategy capacity constrained?
options.B: Has the fund’s track record been audited, and is it long enough for statistical evaluation and inference about the manager’s skill?
options.C: Does the firm manage the fund to specific gross and net exposure targets, and where does the fund stand today versus those targets and why?

Treasury analyst worried that new subscriptions will dilute returns for existing investors in a fast-growing macro fund.

**Concept and theory**

A hedge fund manager earns management fees on assets and incentive fees on performance, so the firm can be return oriented, asset growth oriented or both. question: A member of the investment committee of a Canadian university endowment (CAD 3.1 billion) is reviewing two hedge fund managers. Manager P grants equity in the management company to its portfolio managers, traders and research analysts; Manager Q keeps all equity with its founder. The committee member asks how the ownership theme should be applied. Which statement best describes the appropriate approach?

options.A: Manager Q should be screened out, because equity ownership by the investment team is a required condition for aligning the interests of the team with investors.

Endowment committee member applying the ownership theme to one firm that shares equity and one that does not.

Ownership is about who holds equity in the management company. GARP calls “the participation of the investment team in some form of ownership” “a critical area of differentiation among firms”. loText: Identify themes and questions investors can consider when evaluating a hedge fund manager.
question: An internal auditor at an Australian superannuation fund (AUD 48 billion) is validating the track record section of the fund’s manager evaluation checklist, which was built from the Greenwich Roundtable’s recommendations and related guidance on hedge fund due diligence. Which of the following checklist items is NOT consistent with the questions investors should ask about a manager’s track record?

options.A: Whether the track record is long enough to support statistical evaluation and inference.
options.B: Whether the fund’s returns were affected by the size of the fund over time.
options.C: How the track record relates to the portfolio manager’s experience at previous firms.
options.D: Whether the record excludes periods of market stress, so that unusual episodes do not distort it.

solution:
Internal auditor validating track record checklist items.

**Concept and theory**

A track record is only useful if it is reliable and repeatable. GARP, citing the Greenwich Roundtable, says investors should inquire whether the track record “is comparable to similar strategies, has been audited, and is long enough for statistical evaluation and inference, whether returns were impacted by fund size, and if the team that produced the historical track record is still in place today.” It adds two more questions: “how it performed during periods of market stress and how it relates to the portfolio manager’s experience at previous firms, if applicable.” Schweser’s list matches: peer comparison, third-party audit or verification, sufficient history for trend and attribution analysis, performance  […]

loText: Identify themes and questions investors can consider when evaluating a hedge fund manager.
question: A senior risk analyst at a London life insurer is arranging an on-site visit to a hedge fund in which the insurer may invest GBP 200 million. The fund proposes a single meeting with its head of investor relations, who will walk through the marketing pitch book; it says the CIO and the traders are too busy to meet. Which response is most consistent with the guidance on evaluating a manager’s investment process?

options.A: Accept the meeting, because investor relations staff are best placed to give a consistent, approved message on the investment process.
options.B: Ask to meet in person the actual decision makers and risk takers and staff of mixed seniority, noting that poor access now signals poor access if things go wrong.

Senior risk analyst offered only an investor relations pitch-book meeting.

GARP’s section on the investment process says the questions “should be done in person with as many people of mixed seniority as possible. question: A portfolio manager at a Singapore fund of hedge funds (SGD 5.6 billion) is planning reference checks on two candidates. Fund X was launched 14 months ago by a former proprietary trader at two investment banks. Fund Y has been run by the same founders for 12 years. Which reference-check plan is most consistent with the guidance on evaluating the principals?

options.A: Apply an identical process to both, questioning Fund Y’s founders about employers from the distant past as closely as Fund X’s founder.
options.B: For Fund X, rely on the reference list supplied by the manager, since independently obtained references are needed only for established managers.
options.C: For Fund X, verify bank references, both listed and independently obtained; for Fund Y, focus on motivation, stress behaviour, communication and investor experience.
options.D: For Fund Y, focus on verifying prior employment at the founders’ former banks; for Fund X, focus on the experiences other investors have had over the life of the fund.

solution:
Fund of funds PM planning reference checks for a new manager and an established manager.

**Concept and theory**

GARP: “Newer managers are a bit trickier than established ones. New managers need to have references from previous hedge funds or banks verified, both those that are on the manager’s reference list and those that the investor can obtain independently.” By contrast, “more established managers won’t need to be interrogated about previous firms or employers from the distant past as much as start-ups or firms lacking a reliable track record.” For established managers, focus “more on the manager’s motivation, behavior during crisis or stress periods, ability to communicate to investors, and experiences other investors have had, including both positive and negative over the life of t […]

loText: Identify themes and questions investors can consider when evaluating a hedge fund manager.
question: A risk consultant advising a Dutch pension fund (EUR 900 million hedge fund budget) is conducting reference checks on a portfolio manager who claims to have run the book at her previous fund. Four former colleagues confirm that she made the final trading decisions. Her former head of desk says she mainly implemented ideas generated by others. Which next step is most appropriate?

options.A: Vet the difference of opinion thoroughly and then discuss it directly with the manager, since there is often, but not always, a good explanation.
options.B: Set aside the former head of desk’s view, because the majority of references agree and that consistency removes the need for any follow-up.
options.C: Treat the difference as conclusive evidence of misrepresentation and reject the manager without discussing it with her.
options.D: Ask the fund’s investor relations team to nominate further references who can confirm the manager’s role at her previous fund.

solution:
Consultant facing conflicting references on whether a manager was the decision maker.

**Concept and theory**

Verifying prior employment is “just the beginning”. GARP asks: “Did they do what they described? Were they the trigger puller or acting in a support role? Did they generate ideas or implement ideas? Did they operate individually or within a group?” The best way to find out is to ask former colleagues, partners, managers, clients or other independent parties, treating reference checks “as a 360-degree review of what a person has claimed”. “If enough people are saying the same thing about a person or a firm, then an investor can take some comfort. question: The chief compliance officer of a Brazilian pension fund (BRL 14 billion) receives a background search report on a credit hedge fund manager. The fund charges a 2% management fee and has delivered 11% a year in BRL since launch. The report finds that the fund executes most trades through a broker owned by the manager’s holding company and that its administrator is a subsidiary of the same group. loText: Identify themes and questions investors can consider when evaluating a hedge fund manager.
question:
A risk analyst at a Chinese life insurer (CNY 60 billion of alternatives) is assessing the track record of an Asian equity long/short fund. Her data are below.

| Item | Finding |
|---|---|
| Length of record | 9 years of monthly returns |
| Verification | Returns audited annually by an independent auditor |
| Peer comparison | Top quartile against funds with a similar strategy |
| Stress periods | Drawdowns in 2020 and 2022 in line with peers |
| Assets under management | CNY 0.6 billion in 2017; CNY 9.5 billion today |
| Investment team | Lead PM and two of three analysts behind the 2016 to 2021 returns left in 2023 |
| Fees | 1.75% management fee and 20% incentive fee |

Which two track record questions do her findings most clearly flag for further work?

options.A: Whether the record has been audited, and whether it is long enough for statistical inference.
options.B: Whether the record is comparable to similar strategies, and how it performed under market stress.
options.C: Whether the fee terms are in line with peers, and whether returns were affected by fund size.
options.D: Whether returns were affected by fund size, and whether the team that produced the record is still in place.

solution:
Risk analyst reading a track record data table with excess data.

**Concept and theory**

The track record questions (Solution 5) each guard against a specific failure: comparability (beta mistaken for skill), audit (fabricated returns), length (luck), fund size (scalability), team in place (repeatability), stress (tail risk), and previous firms (unverified skill). Applying them to data means checking which conditions the data show as satisfied and which show as at risk.

**Applying it to this question**

Row by row:

- 9 years of monthly data: long enough; no flag.
- Independent annual audit: satisfied; no flag.
- Top quartile vs similar strategies: comparable; no flag.
- Stress drawdowns in line with peers: no flag.

loText: Explain how due diligence can be performed on a hedge fund’s operational environment.
question: A senior risk analyst at a UK defined benefit pension scheme is presenting to newly hired analysts who will join the scheme’s hedge fund operational due diligence (ODD) team. One slide summarizes the primary purpose of ODD. Which of the following statements best describes that purpose?

options.A: To confirm that the manager’s investment process can generate returns, net of fees, that exceed those of a comparable strategy index over a full market cycle.
options.B: To confirm that management fee revenue covers the management company’s operating expenses, so that the firm can survive a period without performance fees.
options.C: To ensure that no significant additional risk of loss arises for investors from settlement, corporate actions, theft by employees or agents, or breakdowns in confirmation, valuation or reconciliation.
options.D: To ensure that every risk of loss from settlement, corporate actions, theft or reconciliation breakdowns is eliminated before capital is committed, leaving investors with market risk only.

Q1: Presenting to new analysts, which statement best describes the primary purpose of operational due diligence?

Mirabile splits hedge fund due diligence into four parts: investment process, risk management, operational environment, and business model. Each answers a different question. Investment due diligence asks whether the manager can make money; risk management review asks whether the risks taken are understood and controlled; business model review asks whether the management company can survive as a business. Operational due diligence (ODD) asks something narrower and more mechanical: even if the strategy works, can investors lose money through the plumbing of the fund?

question:
An internal auditor at a Canadian fund of hedge funds is validating the ODD file on a target fund (NAV CAD 1.2 billion). The file contains the following notes:

- Background checks were completed on the portfolio manager and two research analysts.
- In the site meeting, the CEO described compliance as “a cost we keep to the legal minimum.”
- The COO and CFO joined three months ago from a global bank; no background checks were run on them.
- The fund has outperformed its peer group in each of the last five years.

Which recommendation by the auditor is most consistent with sound operational due diligence?

options.A: Extend background checks to the COO, CFO and other key back and middle office staff, and record the CEO’s attitude as a significant finding on the fund’s control culture.

loText: Explain how due diligence can be performed on a hedge fund’s operational environment.
question: A risk consultant advising an Australian superannuation fund is on a site visit to a credit hedge fund that seeks an AUD 150 million allocation. The fund hands over a 140-page manual of written procedures covering trading, derivatives, cash and securities processing, and position servicing. The consultant must advise the trustee on how much assurance this provides. Which advice is most accurate?

options.A: The manual’s length and its coverage of trading, derivatives and cash processing give strong assurance that controls are effective, so further control testing is not needed.
options.B: The manual is the best available evidence of control effectiveness, and an outside audit opinion adds little because outside auditors review only whether controls are designed well.
options.C: The manual matters mainly for measuring and monitoring market risk, so its review belongs to the fund’s risk committee rather than to the investor’s operational review.

Q3: Consultant on a site visit is given a 140-page procedures manual; how much assurance does it provide?

Written procedures describe what the fund intends to do. The risk ODD addresses is what the fund actually does each day. GARP notes that reviewing procedures for trading, derivatives, cash and securities processing and position servicing is now routine on site visits, and investors look for evidence of how the written policies are being followed. But such reviews “are not really comprehensive or efficient”; they only give a sense of whether management takes the control process seriously. question: A treasury analyst at a Japanese life insurer is reviewing a global macro fund in which the insurer plans to invest JPY 8 billion. The fund holds all of its excess cash and all up-front margin on its OTC derivatives with a single dealer. The fund reviews that dealer’s credit rating once a month. Which recommendation is most consistent with operational due diligence guidance?

options.A: Spread the exposure across several dealers, move excess cash out of firms that may be at risk, and monitor counterparties daily, since past dealer failures left funds recovering only part of their cash.
options.B: Keep the single dealer, since cash held at a dealer is safe as a receivable on the fund’s balance sheet, provided the monthly rating reviews continue to show investment grade.
options.C: Spread the exposure across several dealers, after which monthly monitoring is sufficient, because diversification across dealers eliminates losses from a dealer default.
options.D: Leave the exposure to the market risk review rather than operational review, since counterparty exposure from OTC derivatives is a market risk issue and not an operational one.

solution:
Q5: Macro fund holds all excess cash and OTC margin at one dealer, monitored monthly; what to recommend?

**Concept and theory**

Counterparty risk from OTC derivatives and other trade counterparties is now a routine part of ODD. A fund that posts up-front margin, or leaves cash with a dealer, holds an unsecured claim on that dealer. GARP’s lesson from the Lehman, MF Global and Refco failures: firms holding up-front margin failed and closed out fund positions without returning the margin. When a dealer goes bust the fund may never get the money back; at a minimum there may be a lengthy court battle, and recovery may only be 30 or 40 percent of an amount the fund thought was safe as cash or a dealer receivable.

loText: Explain how due diligence can be performed on a hedge fund’s operational environment.
question: A member of the risk committee of a Brazilian pension fund is reviewing an ODD report on a BRL 600 million hedge fund. The report notes that the fund’s board consists of the CEO (as chair), the CEO’s long-time business partner, and one independent director appointed last month. Board minutes show that service provider appointments have never been discussed. Two NAV calculation breaks in the past year were logged and closed without root-cause analysis or remediation. Which conclusion is most accurate?

options.A: Governance is adequate because a board exists and includes an independent director, so the unremediated NAV breaks are a matter for the fund’s auditor alone.
options.B: Governance weakness matters only if the NAV breaks caused investor losses; since both breaks were closed, the investor does not need to take further action.
options.C: Governance appears to lack teeth: it does not extend meaningfully beyond the CEO, directors are not engaging with service provider decisions, and breaches are not remedied.
options.D: Governance weakness is a business model risk, so it should be assessed through the fund’s succession plan and key person insurance rather than in the operational review.

solution:
Q6: Board of CEO, his business partner and a new independent director; no discussion of service providers; NAV breaks closed without remediation.

**Concept and theory**

Governance is the last line of the internal control assessment. GARP asks: is there a governance structure that extends beyond the CEO, and if so, does it have any teeth? Investors increasingly hold fund directors and advisors accountable for the decisions a fund manager makes on service providers, and for actions that lead to style drift or even fraud. A board that exists on paper but does not challenge the CEO offers no protection.

Schweser adds a test of effectiveness: is governance pervasive throughout the organization, and are internal control breaches followed up with actions to remedy them and prevent recurrence?  […]

options.B: The mismatch is immaterial to document review, because lock-up and notice terms belong to the risk management review of whether terms fit the strategy.
options.C: The manager’s verbal confirmation settles the matter, because verbal confirmation is the final step of document review and supersedes the written fund documents.
options.D: The mismatch is a red flag: the documents should say the same thing at the same time, and since the offering memorandum governs, the verbal terms must be reconciled to it.

solution:
Q8: Lock-up and notice terms differ between the offering memorandum and the website; manager says the website is current.

**Concept and theory**

Fund terms appear in several documents: the offering memorandum (OM), subscription agreement, limited partnership agreement, investment management agreement, Form ADV and website. GARP says it is very important to ensure that they are all saying the same thing at the same point in time. Documents often change after launch, and some may no longer match the OM, which ultimately governs an investor’s rights and obligations. Particular attention goes to fees, liquidity, side pockets, gates, suspension rights, creation of subfunds or SPVs, and changes in offshore investment managers.

question: A risk analyst at the wealth management arm of a Chinese bank is reviewing the conflicts of interest section of an offering memorandum for a CNY 300 million allocation. The section reads, in full: “Affiliates of the Investment Manager may from time to time have commercial dealings with service providers to the Fund; all such dealings are conducted on normal commercial terms.” Which response is most appropriate?

options.A: Accept the clause, since the assurance that all dealings are on normal commercial terms means that any conflict arising from these relationships has been neutralized.
options.B: Disregard the clause as boilerplate drafted to protect the law firm, since the fund’s real conflicts are normally set out in the risk factors section of the memorandum.
options.C: Query the clause with the manager, since vague wording can cover anything from benign shared services to a personal rebate paid to the manager by a service provider.
options.D: Reject the fund, since any affiliate dealing with a fund service provider is a disqualifying conflict, whatever explanation of the arrangement the manager provides.

solution:
Q9: Vague conflicts of interest clause on affiliates’ dealings with fund service providers.

**Concept and theory**

The conflicts of interest section of the OM is where the drafting law firm most clearly states any concern about nonstandard arrangements with managers, co-investors and others. GARP tells investors to query these representations, especially when they are vaguely worded. GARP’s example is a clause saying certain principals or affiliates may have relationships with fund counterparties but will always deal at arm’s length. loText: Explain how due diligence can be performed on a hedge fund’s operational environment.
question:
A senior risk analyst at a UK insurer is comparing the risk factor sections of three offering memoranda:

- Fund X (leveraged emerging market credit, uses OTC derivatives): four short, generic risk factors on “market conditions” and “general economic risk”; nothing on leverage, derivatives or emerging markets.
- Fund Y (US large-cap long/short equity): 70 pages of risk factors, including risks of real estate development and agricultural commodities.
- Fund Z (merger arbitrage): 18 risk factors, each specific to the strategy.

Which conclusion is most accurate?

options.A: X and Y both raise red flags, X’s more so; Y’s broad and irrelevant factors suggest the law firm drafted mainly to protect itself rather than the investor.
options.B: X and Y both raise red flags, Y’s more so; too many risk factors are more of a red flag than too few, as they bury the material risks of the strategy.
options.C: Only Y raises a red flag; X’s short list is acceptable, because brief risk disclosure normally indicates a simple strategy with few material risks.
options.D: Only X raises a red flag; Y’s long list protects the investor, because the more risks the memorandum discloses, the better informed the investor is.

solution:
Q10: Comparing a very short generic risk section, a very long irrelevant one, and a specific one.

**Concept and theory**

Risk factor disclosure tells the investor how well the drafting law firm understood the manager’s program. GARP: caution is advised when there are either insufficient or extremely broad risk disclosures. Insufficient risk factors are more of a red flag than too many. Overly broad and irrelevant risk factors are also a red flag: the law firm may not have looked properly at the manager’s program, or may be drafting the OM so broadly that it is mainly protecting itself, not the investor. loText: Explain how due diligence can be performed on a hedge fund’s operational environment.
question:
An internal auditor at an Australian insurer is reviewing the limited partnership agreement of a GBP 500 million multi-strategy fund. It contains these clauses:

- Clause 1: The fund indemnifies the manager and directors for all losses from their acts or omissions, other than losses from fraud.
- Clause 2: The manager may invest in any instrument, in any market, with no limit on leverage or concentration.
- Clause 3: The manager may amend this agreement on 10 business days’ notice to investors.
- Clause 4: The manager will deliver audited annual financial statements and report the tax implications of the fund’s investments to investors.

Which of the following assessments is most accurate?

options.A: Clause 1 is consistent with typical practice, because fraud is the carve-out that indemnification provisions are normally expected to contain.
options.B: Clause 2 carries less risk than narrow provisions, because broad powers allow the manager to respond freely as market conditions change.
options.C: Clause 3 is acceptable, because a manager’s right to amend fund documents is a concern only when investors receive no notice of changes.
options.D: Clause 4 is what the investor should expect, because the documents should state the manager’s duties to report audited statements and tax effects.

solution:
Q11: Four limited partnership agreement clauses on indemnification, powers, amendment and reporting.

**Concept and theory**

Beyond terms, the documents define what the manager may do and what it owes investors. GARP’s checklist on the powers of the manager:

- Are the powers very broad or relatively narrow? (Schweser: very broad provisions are potentially more risky.)
- Are there restrictions on leverage or concentration?
- Can the manager amend fund documents, such as the limited partnership agreement?
- What are the key man event rights or notice to investors?
